title: A latent neural ODE learns the dynamics in a few coordinates: encode, evolve, decode, and check what was lost
summary: When many measured variables move together, a map from state to a few latent coordinates can carry the whole motion. A latent neural ODE encodes the state, evolves the latent vector with a small ODE and decodes back. It works when the latent subspace is closed under the dynamics and fails when it is not, or when a new start leaves the span of the training data: both can be measured with a reconstruction error and a latent-consistency error.

On the right, the image of the square under a smooth map: a curved band, with a colour bar for u and a note that the determinant of the Jacobian lies between 0.30 and 1.56.
media.caption: Reference render of plot class F2.1 with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery), not a project result.

source.note: Standard material (autoencoders, projection onto a principal subspace, latent ODE models as in the neural-ODE literature). The figure is the design system's synthetic F2.1 render of a region before and after a map, used as a picture of a map from one coordinate system to another, not as a result. All numbers were computed for this page with NumPy and SciPy on a six-variable linear system with two slow oscillating modes.

read_the_figure.question: How does a map change the shape and size of a region, and where does it squeeze most?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: the domain coordinates u and v from 0 to 1. Right: the image coordinates x and y. Colour is u on both sides, so each point can be followed.
look_at: The colour bands: they stay in order, so the map keeps neighbours together.
Where the grid lines bunch up on the right: the map squeezes there, a small step in latent coordinates covers little of the state.
Whether the image folds over itself (the determinant would change sign); a map that folds cannot be inverted.
The range of the Jacobian determinant in the note: 0.30 to 1.56 means areas change by that factor.
read_the_figure.proves: That this map is smooth, orientation-preserving and locally invertible on this region. An encoder-decoder pair is such a map pair, but the picture does not say how well a decoder reproduces data it was not trained on.
if_wrong: Colour dropped on one side: points cannot be matched between the panels.
Different axis scales between panels without saying so: area change is misread.
Judging a decoder from the image of the training region only: outside it the map may fold.
must_check: Colour represents the same variable in both panels.
Where the determinant of the Jacobian is smallest.

terms.meaning: A short vector z that stands for the full state x: few numbers carrying the motion.
The map from the full state to the latent vector.
The map from the latent vector back to a full state.
An ODE for the latent vector, often a small neural network, integrated with an ordinary solver.
How far decoding the encoding of a state is from the state.
How far the encoded next state is from the latent ODE's prediction from the encoded current state.
A subspace that the dynamics never leave. A latent description is exact only if the decoder's range is invariant.
An initial condition not used in training: the only fair test of a rollout.

remember: A latent neural ODE has three parts: $z_0=E(x_0)$, $\dot z=g_\theta(z)$, $\hat x(t)=D(z(t))$.
Training uses a reconstruction loss $\|x_k-D(E(x_k))\|^2$ and a dynamics loss $\|x_k-D(z(t_k))\|^2$ (or the latent-consistency loss); the two must both be small.
For a linear encoder and decoder the best reconstruction is the principal-subspace projection, with error equal to the discarded singular values (Eckart-Young).
A latent model of a linear system is exact only if the span of the decoder is invariant under the system matrix. A subspace of leading POD modes is not invariant in general.
Reconstruction error is a floor: no latent ODE can do better than the decoder's range allows.
The latent size $r$ must be at least the number of independent modes the data excite (for a rotation with decay: 2 per oscillating pair).

understand.title: Easy: a drawing from a few numbers
understand.text: Imagine describing a swinging gate with two numbers, its angle and speed, instead of the position of every atom. The encoder reads the angle and speed from a photograph, the latent ODE predicts how they change, the decoder redraws the photograph. If two numbers are enough the whole movie becomes a short recipe. If the gate also wobbles in a way two numbers do not capture, the redrawn picture misses the wobble.

understand.title: Medium: two losses with two jobs
understand.text: Reconstruction asks that the pair encoder-decoder loses little. The dynamics loss asks that the evolved latent decodes to the observed future. A model can score well on reconstruction and badly on dynamics if the latent coordinates are well chosen to describe a snapshot but not to be advanced by a simple ODE. The consistency error checks the latent step on its own, before decoding.

understand.title: Hard: closure again
understand.text: With a linear encoder $E=U_r^{\top}$ and decoder $D=U_r$ the latent step is $U_r^{\top}e^{M\Delta t}U_r$. That is exact only when the range of $U_r$ is invariant under $M$. Leading singular vectors of the data are the best fit of a snapshot but are not invariant subspaces of $M$ unless the data came from one. The remainder shows up as a drift in the rollout that grows with the horizon. A nonlinear decoder can curve the subspace to follow the data, but then the latent ODE must carry the curvature.

understand.title: Hardest: generalisation outside the data
understand.text: Both maps are trained on the span of the training trajectories. A new start with a component outside that span is encoded to something that lies in the span, and the rollout answers a different question. The check is a held-out start and a plot of reconstruction error against the distance from the training set. A latent model may also be non-unique: any invertible reparametrisation of $z$ gives an equivalent model, so latent coordinates have no meaning unless fixed by a constraint.

steps.title: Encode, evolve, decode
steps.note: The solver works only on $r$ numbers. The cost per step falls with $r$, and so does the stiffness the solver sees if the fast modes are left out of the latent space.

steps.title: The best linear encoder-decoder is a projection
steps.note: Using the singular value decomposition of the snapshots. A linear autoencoder trained with squared error has the same optimum as this projection (principal component analysis). Nonlinear networks can do better when the data lie on a curved surface, such as the curved band in the figure.

steps.title: A test system with six variables
steps.note: A slow damped oscillation (rates $-0.1\pm i$) plus four decaying modes, mixed by a random matrix $V$. The data from one start have singular values 26.7, 14.0, 1.86, 0.375, 0.109 and 0.0008 (computed, seed 1): two modes carry 99.6 percent of the energy.

steps.title: Reconstruction error is a floor
steps.note: With $r=2$ latent coordinates the relative reconstruction error was 0.0627; with $r=3$ it was 0.0129 (computed). Whatever the latent ODE does, the decoded trajectory cannot be closer to the data than this.

steps.title: The latent step and its consistency
steps.note: A linear latent map fitted by least squares gave a consistency error of 0.0049 for $r=2$ and 0.0014 for $r=3$. The projected exact flow $U_r^{\top}e^{M\Delta t}U_r$ gave the same numbers to six digits, which shows that the remaining error is the non-invariance of the leading subspace and not the fit.

steps.title: Rollout error accumulates
steps.note: Rolled out from the encoded start, the decoded trajectory had a relative error of 0.124 for $r=2$ and 0.0225 for $r=3$ (computed). For $r=2$ the pointwise error was 0.79 at $t=0$, 0.25 at $t=2$, 0.074 at $t=5$ and 0.37 at $t=10$: the start is poorly encoded, the middle is good, and the end drifts. Small per-step inconsistencies grow with the horizon.

steps.title: A new start outside the span
steps.tex: x_0'\notin\operatorname{span}\{x(t_k)\}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{encoding projects it onto a different problem}
steps.note: The same $r=2$ model, applied to a new start that excites the modes differently, had a rollout error of 1.09 (109 percent), with a reconstruction error of 0.215 for the data themselves (computed). The model had learned one trajectory's subspace, not the system. A held-out start is the only test that exposes this.

worked.title: Choose the latent size for the six-variable system and test it from a new start
worked.problem: Use the six-variable system with an oscillating pair and four decaying modes, started so that all modes are excited. Compute POD energy, reconstruction, consistency and rollout error for $r=2$ and $r=3$, and the rollout error from a second start with a different mix of modes.

solution.text: Rollout error from the training start.
Rollout error from a new start with $r=2$.

worked.answer: Two modes carry 99.6 percent of the energy yet the decoded rollout is 12 percent off and the model collapses (109 percent error) from a new start; three modes cut the training rollout error to 2.2 percent. The energy fraction alone would have chosen $r=2$; the rollout and the held-out start show that $r=2$ is not enough. Add a start that excites each mode before trusting any $r$.

analyze.q: A latent model has a reconstruction error of 5 percent and a rollout error of 40 percent. Which part is suspect and what do you compute next?
analyze.hint: Consistency error of the latent step; invariance of the decoder range.

analyze.q: Training is repeated with a different seed and the latent coordinates look completely different but the decoded trajectories agree. Is something wrong?
analyze.hint: Any invertible reparametrisation of z is an equivalent model.

analyze.q: Why can adding a fast decaying mode to the data raise the rollout error of a 2-dimensional latent model even though it carries little energy?
analyze.hint: It couples into the slow modes and the leading subspace is not invariant.

evaluate.q: A paper says the latent model compresses 1000 variables to 3 with 99 percent energy. What do you ask?
evaluate.hint: Held-out starts, rollout horizon, consistency error, whether the energy was computed on the training set only.

evaluate.q: Is a nonlinear autoencoder always better than a linear one?
evaluate.hint: Data on a curved surface versus noise and extrapolation.

create: Design an experiment that plots rollout error against latent size r on held-out starts, and a rule to choose r from it.
Propose a latent-consistency loss for training and say how it differs from the plain dynamics loss.
Sketch a plot that shows where in the state space the decoder stops being accurate.

checks.q: What is the difference between reconstruction error and latent-consistency error?
checks.hint: One concerns a single snapshot, the other one step.
checks.answer: Reconstruction compares a state with the decode of its encoding: it asks whether the latent space can hold the state. Consistency compares the encoded next state with the latent ODE's prediction: it asks whether the latent dynamics are right. Each can be small while the other is large.

checks.q: Two modes hold 99.6 percent of the energy. What is the relative reconstruction error of the best 2-mode linear model?
checks.hint: Square root of the discarded energy.
checks.answer: $\sqrt{1-0.9961}=0.0624$ (calculated), in the check 0.0627 (the energy value is rounded).

checks.q: Why was the pointwise rollout error 0.79 at $t=0$ for $r=2$?
checks.hint: Think of the encoding of the starting state.
checks.answer: At $t=0$ all six modes are excited, so the start has a large component outside the two-dimensional subspace. Encoding discards it, so the decoded start is wrong by about the size of that component. As the neglected modes decay (rates 0.4 to 3) the discarded part vanishes and the error falls to 0.074 by $t=5$.

checks.q: A model is trained on one trajectory and scores 1 percent rollout error on it. Can it be called a model of the system?
checks.hint: What was the set of starts used?
checks.answer: No. It shows that the model can represent that trajectory. In the check the same $r=2$ model had a 109 percent error from a new start. A claim about the system needs starts that were not used in training and that excite the modes differently.

checks.q: Design the loss for a latent neural ODE that avoids a good snapshot encoder with a useless latent dynamics.
checks.hint: Use both terms and the multi-step rollout.
checks.answer: Sum the reconstruction loss, the multi-step rollout loss $\sum_k\|x_k-D(z(t_k))\|^2$ obtained by integrating from $E(x_0)$, and the one-step consistency loss on the latent coordinates. Weight them so that none dominates, use several start times and held-out validation starts, and report all three errors.
